clinicalPearls: Acatalasaemia is an autosomal recessive deficiency of the antioxidant enzyme catalase, encoded by CAT, which normally decomposes hydrogen peroxide within peroxisomes
It was first described in Japan (Takahara disease) and is often clinically silent, discovered incidentally when blood fails to froth on contact with hydrogen peroxide
The best-known manifestation is progressive oral gangrene (Takahara disease), where hydrogen peroxide from oral bacteria is not detoxified, leading to painful ulcerating gum and alveolar lesions
Many individuals, especially those with residual enzyme activity (hypocatalasaemia), remain entirely asymptomatic throughout life
Reduced antioxidant defence has been linked epidemiologically to increased susceptibility to oxidative-stress-related conditions such as diabetes mellitus in some populations
Diagnosis is by demonstrating absent or markedly reduced erythrocyte catalase activity, confirmed by CAT gene analysis
Management centres on scrupulous oral hygiene and prompt treatment of oral infection; no specific enzyme replacement exists
reference.pathophysiology: Acatalasaemia results from recessive loss-of-function mutations in CAT, the gene encoding catalase, a haem-containing peroxisomal enzyme that catalyses the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. When catalase activity is largely absent, hydrogen peroxide generated by cellular metabolism or, in the mouth, by peroxide-producing bacteria is inadequately cleared. The accumulating hydrogen peroxide oxidises haemoglobin and damages tissue, and in the oral cavity it causes local ischaemia and ulceration that manifests as the characteristic gangrenous stomatitis. In most tissues, alternative antioxidant systems such as glutathione peroxidase partly compensate, which explains why many individuals are asymptomatic.
additionalDifferentials: Necrotising (ulcerative) gingivitis and periodontitis of other cause
Immunodeficiency-related oral ulceration and gangrene (for example neutropenia)
Noma (cancrum oris) from severe malnutrition and infection
additionalInvestigations: Erythrocyte catalase activity assay, which is absent or markedly reduced
Simple bedside test observing lack of frothing when blood meets hydrogen peroxide
Full blood count to exclude neutropenia as a cause of oral gangrene
Dental and periodontal assessment of the extent of oral disease
Screening for associated oxidative-stress conditions where clinically indicated
redFlags: Progressive oral gangrene with tissue necrosis and secondary infection
Spreading orofacial infection threatening deeper structures
Severe periodontal destruction with tooth loss
Systemic sepsis arising from an oral focus
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is generally excellent, since most individuals are asymptomatic; where the oral (Takahara) form occurs, outcome is good with meticulous oral hygiene and infection control, and severity tends to lessen after adolescence.
pitfalls: Assuming all affected individuals develop oral disease, when the majority are asymptomatic
Overlooking catalase deficiency as a cause of unexplained recurrent oral gangrene
Failing to distinguish acatalasaemia from neutropenic or malnutrition-related oral necrosis
Not recognising the residual-activity (hypocatalasaemia) state, which is milder and often silent
management: Meticulous oral hygiene and regular periodontal care as the mainstay for preventing and controlling the gangrenous oral disease
Avoid hydrogen-peroxide-containing mouthwashes and topical antiseptics, which cannot be detoxified and aggravate oral ulceration
Prompt debridement and antimicrobial treatment of established oral gangrenous lesions with dental and oral-surgical input
Regular dental and periodontal surveillance, especially during childhood and adolescence when disease activity is greatest
Screen for and manage associated oxidative-stress conditions such as diabetes mellitus where clinically indicated
Reassurance and observation for asymptomatic hypocatalasaemia, with genetic counselling and family testing offered for this autosomal recessive condition
